design_detail: Serial cross-sectional analysis (a four-page research note) of US death certificates in the CDC WONDER Multiple Cause of Death database, 1999–2023, all ages: yearly counts and crude rates per 100,000 population of overdose deaths involving methamphetamine and of those involving cocaine, stratified by sex, race and ethnicity and opioid co-involvement (fentanyl; other opioids), with Joinpoint regression giving annual percentage changes (APC) within segments and an average annual percentage change (AAPC) over the period. Drug involvement is defined by ICD-10 codes listed only in a supplement; 2023 data are provisional.
can_establish: How many US death certificates coded as overdose deaths involving methamphetamine (as the authors define it) there were each year from 1999 to 2023, their crude population rate, and when the growth in these counts sped up or slowed, overall and with or without opioids.
cannot_establish: Death rates among people who use methamphetamine (no denominator of use), that methamphetamine caused the deaths (multiple-cause coding; many deaths involve fentanyl), trends independent of changes in toxicology testing and certification practice, or age-adjusted comparisons (given only in a supplement).

sample.recruitment: Registry: all US death certificates in the CDC WONDER Multiple Cause of Death database, 1999–2023; counts below 10 are suppressed and rates based on fewer than 20 deaths are considered unreliable (p. 1946).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Overdose deaths involving methamphetamine or cocaine, identified by ICD-10 codes given in Supplement 1 (not read) (p. 1946). Because of suppression, the methamphetamine-with-fentanyl series starts in 2003 and the American Indian or Alaska Native series in 2004 (p. 1948); trends for Asian American and Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander people were not assessed because of discrepancies between the preliminary and final databases (Table 1 note 3).
sample.demographics: 2023 methamphetamine-involved deaths: 25,296 men (72.57%) and 9,559 women (27.43%), mean age 45 years (SD 12); cocaine-involved: 73.36% men, mean age 47 (13) (p. 1947).
sample.selection_effects: A complete count of certificates, but deaths whose certificates name no specific drug cannot be attributed, and the authors note possible racial misclassification on death certificates (p. 1948).

exposure.measurement: Drug involvement as coded among the multiple causes on the death certificate; the codes used for methamphetamine are not stated in the article (Supplement 1, not read), so whether the series is the broader code for psychostimulants with abuse potential cannot be checked from the text.
exposure.polysubstance: Stratified by fentanyl and by other opioid co-involvement (Table 1; Figure 1); other drugs are not considered, and the paper does not say whether deaths involving both methamphetamine and cocaine are counted in both series.

comparison.controls: None: descriptive comparisons across years, sex, race and ethnicity and opioid co-involvement.

outcomes.instruments: Death certificates coded with ICD-10 (multiple causes), from CDC WONDER; crude rates per 100,000 population; age-adjusted rates only in eTable 1 (not read) (p. 1946).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not discussed beyond racial misclassification and data suppression (p. 1948). Changes over time in toxicology testing and in how specifically certificates name drugs are not considered.
outcomes.operationalization: Overdose death involving methamphetamine: a death certificate whose multiple-cause codes include the authors' methamphetamine code(s); involvement does not mean that the drug was the cause.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; 18 Joinpoint series (2 drugs by 9 strata, Table 1).

analysis.covariates: None (crude rates); age-adjusted Joinpoint analyses only in eTable 1, not read.
analysis.selective_reporting: Yearly counts are not printed except for 1999 and 2023; the rates by opioid co-involvement and by race and ethnicity are shown only in Figure 1, without printed values.
analysis.power: Not applicable for national counts; early-year subgroup counts are suppressed.

interpretation_gap.results_show: US overdose deaths coded as involving methamphetamine rose about 64-fold in count (547 to 34,855) and 52-fold in crude rate (editors' calculation) from 1999 to 2023, fastest in 2018–2021 (37% a year), then slowed to 3.4% a year in 2021–2023 (provisional 2023 data). Deaths involving methamphetamine with fentanyl grew fastest (76% a year in 2012–2021), and those with other opioids fell in 2021–2023.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract stresses rising stimulant mortality and racial disparities and calls for harm reduction, research funding and targeted interventions (p. 1946); it does not mention that the methamphetamine increase slowed sharply after 2021. Its statement that methamphetamine-involved deaths were highest among American Indian or Alaska Native people is given as a share of their overdose deaths (44.50%); Figure 1C shows their crude rate as the highest too (about 32 per 100,000 in 2023 against about 12 for White people, read from the figure), so this statement is borne out. The discussion's statement that cocaine and methamphetamine accounted for roughly one-third of overdose deaths (p. 1948) is ambiguous: read as a combined share it is not given by the note (deaths involving both drugs are not separated); read as each drug separately, it fits 33.19% and 28.06%.

replication.where_it_stands: A registry description, not a test of a hypothesis: other analyses draw on the same certificates, so agreement among them is not independent replication. A check against a different data system (for example toxicology-based medical-examiner surveillance) would be the meaningful comparison.

funding.declared_conflicts: No potential conflict of interest was reported by the author(s) (p. 1949).
funding.affiliations_note: Virginia Commonwealth University (Medical Scientist Training Program; Epidemiology) and Stanford University School of Medicine (p. 1946).

what_would_settle_it: Toxicology-confirmed death surveillance with standardized testing across states and years, reporting methamphetamine separately from other psychostimulants, with age-adjusted rates and, from surveys of the same years, the number of people who use methamphetamine as a denominator.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: National death-certificate counts are the standard source for this question and the trend is large, but the series is a coded proxy whose definition is not shown in the article, the latest year is provisional, and the note contains internal inconsistencies. It may be cited for the counts and crude rates of certificates coded as methamphetamine-involved overdose deaths by year and for the timing of changes in their growth, labelled as such; not for rates among people who use methamphetamine, not for cause, and not for exact 2023 figures without noting the two versions.

key_findings.finding: Data: CDC WONDER Multiple Cause of Death database; crude mortality rates per 100,000 for methamphetamine- and cocaine-involved overdose deaths, all ages, 1999–2023; drug types by ICD-10 codes listed in Supplement 1; counts below 10 suppressed and rates on fewer than 20 deaths unreliable; Joinpoint regression (version 5.2.0) with APC by segment and AAPC; age-adjusted rates only in eTable 1.

Methamphetamine-involved overdose deaths rose from 547 in 1999 to 34,855 in 2023 (25,296 men, 72.57%; 9,559 women, 27.43%; mean age 45, SD 12); the crude rate rose from 0.20 (95% CI 0.18–0.21) to 10.41 (10.30–10.52) per 100,000, AAPC 18.49% (17.67–20.17).

key_findings.note: The 2021–2023 segment, like every 2021–2023 segment in Table 1, is fitted to three yearly values (2021, 2022 and the provisional 2023), so its estimate is fragile beyond the provisional-data point (editors' reading).

key_findings.locator: Table 1, Opioid co-involvement rows (p. 1947); Results, 2nd paragraph (p. 1948)

key_findings.finding: Stimulants were involved in 7.95% of fentanyl-involved overdose deaths in 1999 (58 of 730), 10.28% in 2011 (274 of 2,666) and 56.67% in 2023 (41,583 of 73,379). No count or share of methamphetamine-involved deaths that also involved opioids is printed; Figure 1A plots their crude rates per 100,000 overall, with fentanyl and with other opioids (values not extracted), and the overlap of the two opioid series is not given.

In 2023 methamphetamine was involved in 33.19% of all overdose deaths (35,126 of 105,826) and in 44.50% of overdose deaths among American Indian or Alaska Native people (785 of 1,764); cocaine in 28.06% (29,692 of 105,826) and in 48.47% among Black people (10,936 of 22,563).
Cocaine-involved overdose deaths rose from 3,822 to 29,449 (crude rate 1.37 to 8.79 per 100,000; AAPC 8.80%, 8.18–9.95).
Figure 1 shows crude rates by opioid co-involvement and by race and ethnicity with shaded 95% intervals; the legend states that 2023 data are provisional. Values were not extracted from the figure.

Limitations named by the authors: possible racial misclassification on death certificates, a limited range of sociodemographic variables, and data suppression (methamphetamine-with-fentanyl deaths available only from 2003, American Indian or Alaska Native deaths only from 2004).

reporting_issues.issue: Two different 2023 counts are given for methamphetamine-involved deaths (34,855 in the abstract and results, p. 1947; 35,126 of 105,826 in the results, p. 1948) and for cocaine-involved deaths (29,449 and 29,692).
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably final against provisional data (Table 1 note 3 mentions both databases, and the Figure 1 legend says 2023 data are provisional); the 2023 figure should be cited with this uncertainty.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 1 the overall AAPC for women in the methamphetamine series (8.54) and for men in the cocaine series (18.61) appear transposed: recomputing each AAPC from its printed segment APCs, weighted by segment length, gives 18.61 for women (methamphetamine) and 8.54 for men (cocaine), and reproduces every other overall AAPC in the table to two decimals (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The printed sex-specific AAPCs should not be cited; by the segments, methamphetamine-involved deaths grew about as fast in women as in men.

reporting_issues.issue: The cocaine segments for Black people are printed as 1999–2006, 2006–2021 and 2012–2023, which overlap; the printed AAPC (9.63) is reproduced only if the middle segment is 2006–2012 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor and not about methamphetamine; a typing error in the segment label.

reporting_issues.issue: The ICD-10 codes defining methamphetamine involvement are given only in a supplement, and the provisional status of 2023 data only in a figure legend.
reporting_issues.consequence: From the article alone, the series cannot be matched to other analyses of the same records, and the 2021–2023 slowdown rests partly on provisional data.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion says cocaine and methamphetamine accounted for roughly one-third of overall overdose deaths (p. 1948), while the results give 33.19% for methamphetamine and 28.06% for cocaine separately; the sentence can be read as a combined share or as each drug separately (with nearly half, respectively, for methamphetamine among American Indian or Alaska Native people, 44.50%, and for cocaine among Black people, 48.47%).
reporting_issues.consequence: The combined share is not given (deaths involving both are not separated) and should not be cited.
